core: The strengths perspective as a deliberate alternative to deficit- and pathology-centered assessment
Origin and attribution: Weick, Rapp, Sullivan and Kisthardt (1989, Social Work); Dennis Saleebey as editor and interpreter; the University of Kansas School of Social Welfare

The working propositions: universal presence of assets; hardship as injurious and also potentially generative; no assumed ceiling on capacity to change; collaboration over expert-directed planning; every environment contains resources
Concrete methods: strengths assessment across life domains, exception questions, scaling questions, goals recorded in the person's own words, behavior-describing rather than person-labeling language
Resilience research as the empirical neighbor and its actual finding (Masten 2001)
Rigor point 1: strengths-based practice is not relentless positivity and does not suspend risk, harm, or safeguarding assessment
Rigor point 2: the responsibilization critique - strengths language can be used to shift responsibility for structural problems onto individuals
Rigor point 3: uneven evidence base; 'strengths-based' names a family of practices rather than one testable intervention
supporting: Solution-focused brief therapy as the source of exception and scaling questions, and its federal Title IV-E Prevention Services Clearinghouse rating
Evidence that terminology affects clinician judgments (Kelly and Westerhoff 2010; NIDA guidance)
UK Department of Health and Social Care strengths-based practice framework as a government statement of what the approach is and is not
Strengths model case management for serious mental illness as the most developed testable version
outOfScope: Ecological and systems framing of person and environment - owned by the person-in-environment topic
Trauma theory, trauma responses, and trauma-informed organizational principles - owned by the trauma-informed care topic
Motivational interviewing technique, spirit, and evidence base - owned by the motivational interviewing topic
Any individualized clinical, diagnostic, treatment, legal, or benefits-eligibility guidance
Full instruction in solution-focused brief therapy as a therapy model
Positive psychology as a research program and its character-strengths instruments

claims.claim: The strengths approach was created at the University of Kansas School of Social Welfare in the early-to-mid 1980s by Professor Charles Rapp with doctoral students including Ronna Chamberlain, Walter Kisthardt and W. Patrick Sullivan, initially for work with adults with psychiatric disabilities in community mental health settings during deinstitutionalization.

The perspective was named and articulated in a 1989 Social Work article by Ann Weick - then dean of the KU School of Social Welfare - with Charles Rapp, W. Patrick Sullivan and Walter Kisthardt; Dennis Saleebey, a KU faculty member from 1987 to 2006, became its best-known interpreter through six editions of his edited volume published between 1992 and 2013.

The perspective's stated principles include that every individual, group, family and community has strengths and resources; that trauma, abuse, illness and struggle may also be sources of challenge and opportunity; that client-set goals and aspirations are honored; that people are served through collaboration as directors of their own helping process; and that the strengths and resources of relationships and environments are to be mobilized.
Strengths-based practice does not require discounting or minimizing the problems people bring; Saleebey treated the 'ignores problems' criticism as serious and answered it in 1996.

In a strengths-based approach, risk is explored with the person and managed collaboratively rather than ignored, and the professional's role is not solely to reduce risk; UK government practice guidance states this explicitly.

Reducing packages of support is not the intended outcome of a strengths-based approach; UK government practice guidance states that working this way is not about giving people less support and services but about providing the right help at the right time.

A published critique argues that the strengths perspective runs close to neoliberal notions of self-help and self-responsibility, can romanticize communities, and can gloss over structural inequalities that constrain individual and social development.

Developmental resilience research finds that resilience is common rather than exceptional and usually arises from the normative operation of ordinary human adaptive systems, with the greatest threats to development being adversities that compromise those protective systems.

Exception questions (asking about times the problem was absent or less severe) and scaling questions (rating on a zero-to-ten scale and identifying what would move the rating) are core solution-focused techniques; the federal Title IV-E Prevention Services Clearinghouse describes solution-focused brief therapy in these terms, gives it an overall rating of Promising, and reports a favorable effect on parent or caregiver mental or emotional health.

The terms used to describe a person affect how professionals judge that person: in a randomized study, clinicians who read a vignette describing a 'substance abuser' attributed more personal responsibility and endorsed more punitive responses than clinicians who read an otherwise identical vignette describing a person with a substance use disorder; federal guidance builds its person-first language recommendations on evidence of this kind.

A 2014 meta-analysis of strengths-based service delivery for severe mental illness pooled five studies with 194 participants and found no effect on level of functioning or quality of life, and its authors reported unclear randomization and blinding, heterogeneous outcome measures, and a lack of clear description of the underlying intervention.

A 2016 critical review of seven intervention studies reported emerging evidence that strength-based approaches improve outcomes including hospitalization rates, employment and educational attainment, and intrapersonal outcomes such as self-efficacy and sense of hope, while concluding that further high-quality research is needed.

'Strengths-based' functions as a label for a family of practices - an assessment format, a case management model, a conversational style, an agency philosophy - so evidence attaches to particular programs rather than to the label as a whole.
A strengths-based approach is a stance or approach rather than an outcome or a fixed process, and there is no single model, tool, or technique that constitutes it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether strengths-based service delivery improves outcomes for people with serious mental illness.
positions: Ibrahim, Michail and Callaghan (2014) pooled five studies (n=194) and found no effect on level of functioning or quality of life, with a symptom comparison that did not favor the strengths condition; they rated the evidence moderate quality and the number of trials low.
Tse and colleagues (2016) reviewed seven intervention studies and reported emerging evidence of benefit on hospitalization, employment and education, and self-efficacy and hope.
Saleebey (1996) asserted that strengths-based case management with people with severe mental illness was already well established.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports both reviews explicitly rather than choosing a side, and states that the pooled evidence is thin and the interventions inconsistently described. Saleebey's 1996 assertion is treated as an in-period claim by an advocate, not as an evidence finding, and is not repeated as fact.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the strengths perspective is complicit in shifting responsibility for structural problems onto individuals.
positions: Gray (2011) argues the perspective's affinity with self-help and self-responsibility risks glossing over structural inequality and romanticizing communities.
The UK Department of Health and Social Care handbook (2019) states that reduction of support packages is not the aim and that the approach is not about giving people less.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are reported. The lesson frames the critique as a real failure mode of implementation that official guidance explicitly disclaims, and gives students a concrete test: whether the requested resource was actually offered.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which enumeration of the perspective's principles is authoritative.
positions: The University of Kansas School of Social Welfare publishes an eight-item statement of principles referencing Weick and colleagues (1989).
Saleebey's edited textbook is widely cited for a six-proposition list including 'we do not know the upper limits of the capacity to grow and change' and 'every environment is full of resources'.
A LibreTexts open human-services text lists seven principles drawn from several sources.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not present any single numbered canonical list. It describes the propositions in original wording, attributes the formulation to Saleebey and the Kansas group generally, and supports each proposition with the sources that state it. Saleebey's book text could not be accessed directly, so no wording from it is reproduced or attributed as a quotation.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims about the strengths perspective at all - its body text was subject-agnostic boilerplate ('a foundational concept in Social Work & Human Services', 'a label on a toolbox drawer') that named no originators, no propositions, no methods, and no evidence.
The draft's vocabulary entries ('context', 'evidence', 'application') were generic study-skills terms rather than terminology of this topic, and its definition of the headline term was circular.
The draft implied the topic is a definition to be recited and applied to 'a simple scenario', which understates a perspective that carries a documented critique and a contested evidence base.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all boilerplate prose with sourced content: attribution to Weick, Rapp, Sullivan and Kisthardt (1989) and to Saleebey and the Kansas school.
Added the propositions in precise form, including the 'also' qualifier on hardship so the model is not read as claiming adversity is beneficial.
Added concrete methods (strengths assessment, exception questions, scaling questions, goals in the person's own words, behavior-describing language) with sources.

Added the resilience literature with its actual finding - resilience is common and produced largely by ordinary protective systems and relationships - rather than as a claim about exceptional individual character.
Added the three required rigor points: risk and safety assessment continue unchanged; the responsibilization critique; the uneven and heterogeneous evidence base.
Removed the draft's implied certainty about effectiveness and replaced it with the two divergent reviews reported side by side.
Scoped out ecological framing, trauma content, and motivational interviewing technique, which belong to parallel topics in this subject's queue.
rightsIssues: The University of Kansas principles page is copyrighted institutional content with no reuse licence; used as REFERENCE_ONLY and its enumerated wording is not reproduced.

Saleebey's textbook formulation of the six propositions could not be accessed in a rights-clear form; the lesson therefore describes the propositions in original wording and does not quote or reproduce any numbered list attributed to him.

The UK Department of Health and Social Care handbook PDF contains no licence statement in the document itself. Although gov.uk material is commonly released under the Open Government Licence, that was not verified on the artifact, so the record is REFERENCE_ONLY with no licence asserted.
The BMC Psychiatry meta-analysis is CC BY 4.0; it is cited with attribution and its findings are restated in original wording rather than quoted.
The LibreTexts page declares no licence ('not declared'), so it is REFERENCE_ONLY despite being an open education resource.

Paywalled scholarly sources (Weick 1989, Saleebey 1996, Gray 2011, Tse 2016, Kelly and Westerhoff 2010, Masten 2001) were verified through Crossref metadata, publisher abstracts, and indexing records; no full-text prose from them is reproduced.

Gray (2011) was verified from its Crossref record and publisher abstract; the open-access repository copy returned HTTP 403 and could not be read, so the lesson states only the argument summarized in the abstract.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of the Strengths Perspective
sourceRecords.provider: University of Kansas School of Social Welfare
sourceRecords.notes: Institutional statement of the perspective's principles from the school where it was developed; cites Weick, Rapp, Sullivan and Kisthardt (1989). Used to verify the content of the propositions (universal assets, hardship as challenge and opportunity, client-set goals, collaboration and client direction, mobilizing environmental resources, linking goals to doable actions). Wording paraphrased, not reproduced; page carries a University of Kansas copyright notice and no reuse licence.

sourceRecords.title: History of Strengths Perspective at KU
sourceRecords.provider: University of Kansas School of Social Welfare
sourceRecords.notes: Institutional history from the originating school. Supports the dating and personnel claims: created in the early-to-mid 1980s by faculty and doctoral students including Charles Rapp, Ronna Chamberlain, Walter Kisthardt and W. Patrick Sullivan; first applied with adults with psychiatric disabilities in community mental health during deinstitutionalization; named and articulated in the 1989 Social Work essay by Dean Ann Weick and colleagues; Dennis Saleebey's six editions of his edited volume, 1992-2013. Copyrighted page with no reuse licence; used as reference only and the lesson's wording is original. Note this is the perspective's home institution, so it is a partisan source on the perspective's merits and is used here only for historical facts about its own development.

sourceRecords.title: A Strengths Perspective for Social Work Practice (Social Work, 34(4), 350-354)
sourceRecords.provider: Weick, A., Rapp, C., Sullivan, W. P., & Kisthardt, W. / Oxford University Press
sourceRecords.notes: Origin article for the strengths perspective. Bibliographic details (authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages, 1989) verified through the Crossref API record; the full text is paywalled, so this source supports only the attribution and dating claim in the lesson, corroborated by the KU School of Social Welfare page.

sourceRecords.title: The Strengths Perspective in Social Work Practice: Extensions and Cautions (Social Work, 41(3), 296-305)
sourceRecords.notes: Saleebey's own review of endorsements and criticisms of the perspective. Supports the lesson's statement that the approach does not mandate discounting people's problems and that he treated the 'ignores problems' criticism as serious. Publisher abstract page verified; full text paywalled and not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The strengths based approach as a service delivery model for severe mental illness: a meta-analysis of clinical trials (BMC Psychiatry, 14:243)
sourceRecords.provider: Ibrahim, N., Michail, M., & Callaghan, P. / BMC Psychiatry
sourceRecords.notes: Open-access meta-analysis. Supports the lesson's evidence paragraph: five studies pooled (four RCTs, one quasi-experimental), 194 participants, no significant effect on level of functioning or quality of life, moderate-quality evidence, low trial count, and explicit criticism of unclear randomization/blinding, heterogeneous measures, and the lack of clear description of the underlying intervention. Findings restated in original wording; no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Uses of strength-based interventions for people with serious mental illness: A critical review (International Journal of Social Psychiatry, 62(3), 281-291)
sourceRecords.provider: Tse, S., Tsoi, E. W. S., Hamilton, B., O'Hagan, M., Shepherd, G., Slade, M., Whitley, R., & Petrakis, M. / SAGE
sourceRecords.notes: Critical review of seven intervention studies (2001-2014). Supports the lesson's statement that there is emerging evidence of benefit on hospitalization rates, employment and educational attainment, and self-efficacy and hope, alongside the authors' conclusion that higher-quality research is still required. Citation and abstract verified via the Crossref record; full text not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Back to Basics: A Critique of the Strengths Perspective in Social Work (Families in Society, 92(1), 5-11)
sourceRecords.provider: Gray, M. / Families in Society: The Journal of Contemporary Social Services
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the responsibilization critique in the lesson: the perspective's proximity to neoliberal self-help and self-responsibility, its tendency to romanticize communities, and its glossing over of structural inequality. Bibliographic details verified via Crossref; argument verified from the publisher abstract. Publisher and repository full texts returned HTTP 403, so no full-text detail beyond the abstract is asserted.

sourceRecords.title: Ordinary Magic: Resilience Processes in Development (American Psychologist, 56(3), 227-238)
sourceRecords.provider: Masten, A. S. / American Psychological Association, indexed by ERIC (EJ627466)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the resilience paragraph: resilience is common, usually arises from the normative functions of human adaptational systems, and the greatest threats to development are those that compromise those protective systems. Abstract and full citation verified through the ERIC record; article text paywalled and not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Solution-Focused Brief Therapy - program review
sourceRecords.provider: Title IV-E Prevention Services Clearinghouse, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
sourceRecords.notes: Federal clearinghouse review. Supports the description of solution-focused technique (cooperative alliance, identifying exceptions when the problem was less severe, rating progress on a zero-to-ten scale, ending sessions with suggested actions) and the Promising rating with a favorable effect for parent or caregiver mental or emotional health. Used as reference only; no text reproduced and no reuse right inferred from the domain.

sourceRecords.title: Words Matter: Preferred Language for Talking About Addiction
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the lesson's language-choice method: person-first phrasing separates the person from the condition, stigmatizing terms reduce willingness to seek help and lower a person's sense of hope and self-efficacy, and federal guidance recommends describing condition or behavior rather than labeling people. Used as reference only; wording not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Does it matter how we refer to individuals with substance-related conditions? A randomized study of two commonly used terms (International Journal of Drug Policy, 21(3), 202-207)
sourceRecords.provider: Kelly, J. F., & Westerhoff, C. M. / Elsevier
sourceRecords.notes: Randomized comparison of the terms 'substance abuser' and 'having a substance use disorder' in an otherwise identical vignette; participants attributed more personal responsibility and endorsed more punitive responses under the labeling term. Bibliographic details verified via Crossref and the finding corroborated by NIDA guidance. Supports the lesson's claim that descriptive language changes professional judgment. Full text paywalled and not reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Strengths-based approach: Practice Framework and Practice Handbook (February 2019)
sourceRecords.provider: Department of Health and Social Care (United Kingdom), with the Chief Social Worker for Adults
sourceRecords.notes: UK government practice guidance for adult social care, read in full via local text extraction. Supports: the approach challenges the deficit model and explores the person's whole circumstances collaboratively; risk is explored with the person and managed rather than treated as a barrier, and the professional's role is not solely to reduce risk; reduction of support packages is not the sought outcome and the approach is not about giving people less; a strengths-based approach is an approach rather than an outcome or process, with no single required model or tool. The PDF contains no licence statement, so no reuse right is asserted; all wording in the lesson is original. UK-specific statutory framing (Care Act 2014) is referenced generically as 'UK practice guidance' and not presented as U.S. law.

sourceRecords.title: 3.4: Strengths-Based Perspective, in Introduction to Human Services (Western Technical College)
sourceRecords.provider: Social Sci LibreTexts / Ashley Patros and Keri Grokowsky
sourceRecords.notes: Open education resource used to corroborate the standard teaching formulation of the principles: people have capacity to learn, grow and change; communities and environments contain abundant resources; providers collaborate with clients; self-determination and empowerment; problems arise from interactions between systems rather than deficits within individuals. The page declares no licence ('not declared'), so it is treated as reference only and no wording is reused.
